<ConflictType> — Conflicting opinions and research outcomes due to differing interpretations of small calorie differences and study designs

Evidence clusters into two main positions. High-credibility sources d1, d9, d10, d11, and d12 report that substituting standing for sitting burns only about 0.15–8 extra calories per minute (roughly 54–88 calories per hour), concluding this is too small to cause meaningful weight loss. In contrast, d6 and d7 cite the same Mayo Clinic–based estimate (54 extra calories over six hours) but frame it as potentially contributing to modest long-term weight loss if diet is unchanged. Other sources (d2, d3, d4, d5, d8) acknowledge small calorie increases and suggest standing may aid weight management or complement exercise, but they stop short of claiming reliable weight loss from standing alone.

The cited evidence collectively shows that standing desks do increase energy expenditure relative to sitting, yet the magnitude is modest and research interpretations diverge on whether that translates into clinically relevant weight loss.

Using a standing desk increases daily calorie expenditure by roughly 54–88 calories compared with sitting, depending on the study and individual factors [d1,d6,d9,d10,d11,d12]. Some analyses project that over years this could lead to modest weight loss if diet remains unchanged, while the majority of high-credibility reviews conclude the effect is too small to produce significant or reliable weight loss on its own [d1,d9,d10,d11,d12]. Several sources note that pairing standing with intentional movement (e.g., walking or desk exercises) yields greater calorie burn and is more likely to support weight-loss goals than standing alone [d5,d8,d10].
